intro: Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen constraints, and the game has to honor all of them. Today's roll was seed 3394538433. Here is each roll and what came of it.

rolls.value: an owl night-shift nurse · tuning · bells
rolls.became: Owls are awake all night anyway, so Nurse Hoo works nights on a children's ward. (The dice first said rubber ducks, but a squid had just squished those four days earlier, so the bells got the job.) Owls and bells go back a long way: belfries. A hospital at 3am is full of things nobody is listening to, a little bell tuned to a note is an instrument, and enough of them hidden in the right places turn the whole building into one.

Hoo hangs each bell on a physio band strung across a tongue-depressor slingshot. A bell on a tighter band rings higher, so you drag it back, listen to the ting climb, and let go on a line of the gauge. The bell flies into the prank on the blueprint.

A ward door that goes “shh-boop”. A tea trolley that plays a chord only when it's carrying biscuits. A lift that politely plays “going up” all the way down to the basement. Eleven pranks in all, each one drawn up as a sheet of plans.

The Toy Fund is three pence a night, and a gift-shop bell costs three pence. So Hoo returns abandoned wheelchairs for their one-penny coin-lock deposits, writes strongly worded memos, and accepts the jingle bells off half-asleep children's slippers.
Bramble Ward, and Matron Bramble: a tall grey heron who signs the Toy Fund, underlines things, and comes out of her office whenever a call light goes unanswered.

rolls.value: automation you program (an action queue with priorities)
rolls.became: Hoo's clipboard. She does the first ticked chore she can, top to bottom, and only remembers a few at once. Put the call lights first or someone wakes up singing. Wheelchairs run “until 20p”, bells get bought to “keep 2”: the order is the program.

rolls.value: a mid-game rule change that reshapes everything
rolls.became: The fifth prank is Matron's own chair, which plays a polka at the six o'clock handover in front of the entire day shift. Mortified, she cuts the Toy Fund to nothing and pulls the coin locks off the wheelchairs. Money stops. Everything costs favours now, and without a budget nothing gets replaced, so old bands go slack and their bells ring flat (♭).

The porters were at handover too. It was the funniest thing they'd seen all year, so the night staff volunteer: bats, hedgehogs and mice you move between Scrounge, Tune, Hush and Cover. Covering each other's breaks is how favours get made.

Hoo drew six lines on her gauge, because the whole-tone scale has six notes. But let go exactly between two lines and the bell clonks: the other six notes, the other whole-tone scale. The later sheets have “?” slots sitting between the lines.
Everything is small: three pence a night, a dozen night staff, ninety-eight bells in eleven pranks. A good night is eleven pence.

About three hours over a few sittings, counted in night shifts. When you come back, Hoo has kept to her clipboard and the staff have kept at it (gently: the ward sleeps through, so there are no bells while you're away).
The whole game is Hoo's plans: the ward drawn from above in white line on blue, every prank a numbered sheet, the gauge sketched on the back of a fluid chart.
Eight colours: two navies for the paper, a slate and a mauve for the shadows, and the warm end (rust, orange, peach, cream) for the ink, the bells and the light by every bed.

The 3am Polka: oom-pah on tiptoe, a tuba-ish bass on the beat and accordion-ish chords off it, over two augmented chords. Whole tone makes it sound like a dream sequence that's a bit tipsy. It goes very quiet when Matron is on the ward, and every bell rings on the same scale, until one clonks.
Nobody gets told off for long. Children ask for water, stories and bells. Hoo says “for inventory” a lot.

rolls.value: one last purchase that costs everything
rolls.became: Discharge morning: unhook every bell from every prank in the hospital and give them all away. It costs everything you have, every bell, every favour and every penny in the jar.

Pip in Bed 4 asked “is there a bell for me?” on the very first night. The Name-Tag Gun, the Gift Wrap Just in Case and the Bed Chart of Notes were silly purchases at the time. On discharge morning every child goes home with a bell in their coat pocket, labelled, wrapped and tuned to their favourite note, jingling all the way to the car park. Pip gets the first one, an E. Matron hums.

outro: None of these were chosen; all of them were rolled. The fun is finding the one story where they all make sense.
